questions.q: Which transport protocol guarantees ordered, reliable delivery of bytes?
questions.why: TCP retransmits lost packets and reorders them; UDP sends datagrams with no delivery or ordering guarantees.

questions.q: Why might a live video call or multiplayer game prefer UDP over TCP?
options: A late packet is useless, so retransmitting it only adds delay
questions.why: For real-time media, dropping a late frame is better than waiting for TCP to retransmit it and stall everything behind it.

questions.q: What does a Layer 7 load balancer look at that a Layer 4 one does not?
options: HTTP details such as the path, headers and cookies
The IP address and port only
questions.why: Layer 7 balancers understand the application protocol, so they can route /api and /images differently or use cookies for stickiness.

questions.q: Which is the main reason to choose a Layer 4 load balancer?
options: It is cheaper and faster and can pass through long-lived connections such as WebSockets
questions.why: Layer 4 forwards TCP/UDP connections without parsing them, which is fast and works for any protocol, including persistent connections.

questions.q: What does DNS do in a request's journey?
options: Turns a hostname into an IP address
questions.why: DNS resolves names like api.example.com to IP addresses; it can also do coarse load balancing by returning different IPs.

questions.q: Server-Sent Events (SSE) are best described as…
options: A one-way stream of updates from server to client over HTTP
A way to send files peer to peer
questions.why: SSE keeps an HTTP response open and pushes events to the client; the client can't send messages back on the same channel.

questions.q: When are WebSockets the better fit than SSE?
options: When both client and server send frequent messages, such as chat
When the server sends a daily report
When you only need to download a file
When responses must be cached by a CDN
questions.why: WebSockets give a full-duplex connection, ideal when both sides talk often; SSE is simpler when only the server pushes.

questions.q: What is long polling?
options: The client asks for updates and the server holds the request open until there is something new
The client polls every second forever
The server opens a connection to the client
questions.why: Long polling reduces empty responses compared with regular polling by keeping each request open until data arrives or a timeout passes.

questions.q: Why is gRPC popular for service-to-service calls inside a system?
options: Compact binary messages (Protocol Buffers), strict contracts and HTTP/2 streaming
It is the only protocol browsers support
questions.why: gRPC is efficient and strongly typed, which suits internal traffic; REST/JSON is still common for public, browser-facing APIs.

questions.q: A client times out calling a payment service. What makes retrying safe?
options: An idempotency key, so a repeated request isn't processed twice
A bigger timeout on the load balancer only
questions.why: The first request may have succeeded before the timeout. Idempotency keys let the server recognise and ignore duplicates; exponential backoff with jitter avoids retry storms.

questions.q: In REST, which method should be used to create a new resource whose ID the server assigns?
questions.why: POST to a collection (POST /tweets) creates a resource and the server chooses its ID. PUT is for replacing a resource at a known URL.

questions.q: Which HTTP methods are expected to be idempotent?
questions.why: Repeating GET, PUT or DELETE leaves the same state. POST usually creates something new each time, so it needs an idempotency key to be retried safely.

questions.q: Which is the most RESTful URL for one user's orders?
questions.why: REST models resources as nouns in the path and uses the HTTP method as the verb.

questions.q: Why is cursor-based pagination preferred over offset pagination for a fast-changing feed?
options: New items don't shift the pages, so you don't see duplicates or skip items, and it stays fast deep into the list
It is easier to jump to page 500
questions.why: A cursor (for example 'items older than this timestamp/ID') is stable as data changes and avoids scanning large offsets. Offsets are fine for small, stable lists.

questions.q: What is GraphQL's main advantage?
options: Clients fetch exactly the fields they need, from several resources, in one request
It is always faster than REST
It removes the need for a database
questions.why: GraphQL avoids over- and under-fetching, which helps varied clients such as mobile apps. It adds complexity in caching and query cost control.

questions.q: Where should the identity of the current user come from in an API?
options: A validated auth token (e.g. JWT or session), not a user ID in the request body
A userId field the client sends
questions.why: Anything in the body can be forged. The server derives who the caller is from authentication, then checks what they're allowed to do.

questions.q: Which status code fits 'you are sending requests too fast'?
questions.why: 429 signals rate limiting, often with a Retry-After header telling the client when to try again.

questions.q: How should an API evolve without breaking existing clients?
options: Add optional fields and version breaking changes (e.g. /v2 or a version header)
questions.why: Additive changes are backward compatible; breaking changes go behind a new version so old clients keep working.

questions.q: In an interview, what should the API section usually cover?
options: The main endpoints for each functional requirement, with inputs and outputs
questions.why: A short list of endpoints that maps to the core requirements shows the contract between client and system; details can come later.

questions.q: Why return 202 Accepted for a request that starts a long video transcoding job?
options: The work continues asynchronously; the client polls or gets notified when it's done
It forces the client to retry
questions.why: 202 tells the client the request was accepted for processing but isn't complete, often with a URL to check the job's status.

questions.q: When is a relational database (like PostgreSQL) a strong default?
options: Structured data with relationships and a need for transactions
When you need no schema at all
questions.why: Relational databases give joins, constraints and ACID transactions, which fit most business data. Reach for other stores when a specific need demands it.

questions.q: What does normalisation aim to reduce?
options: Duplicated data and the update anomalies it causes
questions.why: Normalised tables store each fact once. Denormalisation deliberately duplicates data to make reads faster, at the cost of keeping copies in sync.

questions.q: Why might you denormalise, for example storing a like_count on a post?
options: To avoid an expensive count or join on every read of a read-heavy screen
questions.why: Precomputed values make hot reads cheap; the trade-off is updating them on every write and handling drift.

questions.q: In a key-value or wide-column store like DynamoDB or Cassandra, what should drive the schema?
options: The access patterns: the queries you need to serve
The number of columns in the UI
questions.why: These stores can't join or query arbitrary fields efficiently, so you design keys around how data will be read.

questions.q: A 'user follows user' relationship with millions of users is best modelled as…
options: A follows table (follower_id, followee_id) with indexes in both directions
A comma-separated list in the users table
One row per user with 10,000 follower columns
A JSON file per user on disk
questions.why: A join table scales and supports both 'who do I follow' and 'who follows me' with the right indexes.

questions.q: What is a good partition (shard) key?
options: One that spreads traffic evenly and keeps data that's queried together in one place
The creation date for every table
A value that almost every row shares
questions.why: Low-cardinality or time-based keys create hot partitions. A high-cardinality key aligned with the main query balances load.

questions.q: Where should large binary files such as videos be stored?
options: In object storage (e.g. S3), with only the metadata and URL in the database
questions.why: Object storage is cheap, durable and built for large blobs; databases handle the metadata and queries.

questions.q: What does a foreign key constraint give you?
options: The database refuses references to rows that don't exist
questions.why: Referential integrity is enforced by the database rather than hoped for in application code.

questions.q: Which store fits 'find all friends of friends within 3 hops' best?
options: A graph database, or a relational DB with careful queries at small scale
questions.why: Graph databases are built for traversals. In interviews, a relational model is often fine unless traversal is the core problem.

questions.q: In an interview's 'core entities' step, what do you list?
options: The main nouns the system stores and how they relate (e.g. User, Tweet, Follow)
questions.why: Naming entities early anchors the API and the data model; columns and indexes are refined later.

questions.q: In the cache-aside pattern, who loads data into the cache on a miss?
options: The application: read from the DB, then write to the cache
questions.why: Cache-aside (lazy loading) is the most common pattern: check the cache, fall back to the database, then populate the cache.

questions.q: What does write-through caching do?
options: Writes go to the cache and the database together, keeping the cache fresh
Writes go only to the cache and are lost on restart
questions.why: Write-through keeps cache and DB in step at the cost of slower writes; write-behind writes to the DB later, risking loss.

questions.q: What is a cache stampede (thundering herd)?
options: Many requests miss at once when a hot key expires and all hit the database
A cache that grows too large
questions.why: Fixes include request coalescing (one request refreshes, others wait), staggered TTLs and refreshing hot keys before they expire.

questions.q: Which eviction policy removes the item that hasn't been used for the longest time?
questions.why: LRU keeps recently used items; LFU keeps frequently used ones. LRU is the usual default.

questions.q: What problem does a TTL (time to live) mainly address?
options: Stale data: entries expire so they're reloaded eventually
questions.why: TTLs bound how stale cached data can get and let unused entries age out.

questions.q: What is a CDN best at caching?
options: Static and rarely changing content (images, video, scripts) close to users
Per-user private messages that change every second
questions.why: CDNs serve content from edge locations near users, cutting latency and origin load.

questions.q: How do you keep a cached value correct after the underlying data changes?
options: Invalidate or update the cache entry on writes, and keep a TTL as a safety net
questions.why: Invalidation on write plus a TTL is the practical combination; perfect consistency with a cache is hard, so decide how stale is acceptable.

questions.q: A single celebrity's profile is read millions of times per second. What helps most?
options: Replicating the hot key or adding a small in-process cache in front of the shared cache
questions.why: One key lives on one cache node, which becomes a hotspot. Local caches or key replication spread the load.

questions.q: When is caching a poor fit?
options: When data must always be exactly up to date and is rarely re-read
For computed results that are expensive
questions.why: Caching pays off when the same data is read repeatedly and some staleness is acceptable.

questions.q: Redis is often used as a cache because it…
options: Keeps data in memory with sub-millisecond reads and supports expiry
questions.why: In-memory storage with TTLs and rich data structures makes Redis the default distributed cache in interviews.

questions.q: Why shard a database?
options: One machine can no longer hold the data or handle the write load
questions.why: Sharding splits data across machines to scale storage and writes; read replicas alone only scale reads.

questions.q: What is the main risk of range-based sharding on a timestamp?
options: All new writes land on the newest shard, creating a hotspot
questions.why: Recent data is usually the busiest, so ranges by time concentrate load. Hashing the key spreads writes.

questions.q: What does hash-based sharding give up compared with range sharding?
questions.why: Hashing scatters neighbouring keys, so 'all orders from last week' has to ask every shard.

questions.q: Why is choosing a shard key so important?
options: It decides load balance and which queries stay on one shard; changing it later is expensive
questions.why: A bad key causes hotspots or scatter-gather queries, and resharding means moving lots of data.

questions.q: What is a cross-shard (scatter-gather) query?
options: A query that must ask many shards and merge the results
A query that uses one index
questions.why: They are slower and less reliable, so the shard key should keep the most common queries on a single shard.

questions.q: Which technique reduces data movement when shards are added?
questions.why: With hash % N, changing N remaps most keys; consistent hashing moves only a small fraction.

questions.q: How do you keep 'all messages in a chat' fast in a sharded system?
options: Shard by chat ID so a conversation lives on one shard
Put each message on a random shard
questions.why: Co-locating data that's read together avoids scatter-gather queries.

questions.q: What becomes harder once data is sharded?
options: Transactions and joins that span shards
Reading one row by its key
Adding an index on one shard
questions.why: Cross-shard transactions need distributed coordination (e.g. two-phase commit or sagas), which is complex and slow.

questions.q: A directory-based sharding scheme stores…
options: A lookup table mapping keys (or ranges) to shards
questions.why: A directory adds flexibility (you can move keys) but is another component that must be fast and highly available.

questions.q: Before sharding, what should you usually try first?
options: Indexes, caching, read replicas and a bigger machine
Rewriting the app in another language
questions.why: Sharding adds lasting complexity; many systems scale far with vertical scaling, caching and replicas.

questions.q: What problem does consistent hashing solve?
options: Adding or removing a node remaps only a small fraction of keys
It removes the need for replicas
questions.why: With simple hash mod N, changing N moves almost every key. On a hash ring, only keys between neighbours move.

questions.q: On a consistent hash ring, which node owns a key?
options: The first node found clockwise from the key's position
The node with the most memory
The node with the smallest ID
questions.why: Keys and nodes are hashed onto the same ring; a key belongs to the next node clockwise.

questions.q: Why use virtual nodes?
options: Each physical node takes many positions on the ring, spreading load evenly
questions.why: With few nodes, ranges are uneven. Many virtual positions per node smooth the distribution and share the load of a failed node.

questions.q: When a node leaves the ring, where do its keys go?
questions.why: Only the departing node's ranges move to its successors; the rest of the ring is untouched.

questions.q: Which systems commonly use consistent hashing?
options: Distributed caches and databases like Cassandra and DynamoDB
questions.why: It's the standard way to spread keys across a changing set of cache or storage nodes.

questions.q: How are replicas usually placed on a hash ring?
options: On the next N distinct nodes clockwise
On a random node each read
questions.why: Walking clockwise to the next distinct physical nodes gives replicas without an extra directory.

questions.q: With hash(key) % 4 and 4 servers, adding a 5th server moves roughly…
questions.why: Changing the modulus changes almost every key's result. Consistent hashing would move about 1/5 of them.

questions.q: What is a 'hot key' problem that consistent hashing alone does not fix?
options: One very popular key overwhelming its single owner node
questions.why: Hashing spreads different keys, not traffic to one key. Replicate hot keys or add local caching.

questions.q: Consistent hashing is mainly about…
options: Stable placement of keys across a changing set of nodes
questions.why: Despite the name, it's about key placement, not the C in CAP.

questions.q: In an interview, when is it worth mentioning consistent hashing?
options: When designing a distributed cache or store whose nodes scale up and down
questions.why: It shows you know how to add capacity without reshuffling all data.

questions.q: According to CAP, during a network partition a distributed system must choose between…
questions.why: Partitions happen, so the real choice is: return possibly stale data (available) or refuse until nodes agree (consistent).

questions.q: Which system should favour consistency?
options: A ticket booking system where two people must not buy the same seat
questions.why: Double-selling is unacceptable, so it's better to reject or wait than to show wrong availability.

questions.q: Which system can favour availability?
options: Showing a user's profile picture or follower count
Selling the last item in stock
questions.why: Slightly stale data is harmless there, and staying up matters more.

questions.q: What does 'eventual consistency' mean?
options: If writes stop, all replicas converge to the same value over time
Reads are always up to date
questions.why: Replicas may briefly disagree, which is fine for many features and allows higher availability and lower latency.

questions.q: A good way to present CAP in an interview is to…
options: Decide per feature: e.g. strong consistency for bookings, eventual for browsing
Say the whole system is CA
Claim you can have all three always
questions.why: Real systems mix guarantees; stating which parts need consistency shows judgement.

questions.q: 'Read-your-own-writes' consistency guarantees that…
options: After you update something, you see your change, even if others see it later
Reads come only from the leader for all users
questions.why: It's a common middle ground: route a user's reads to the leader (or a fresh replica) briefly after their writes.

questions.q: Which technique gives strong consistency for a single record in a replicated database?
options: Reads and writes go through a leader, or use quorum reads/writes
questions.why: A single leader, or overlapping quorums (R + W > N), ensures reads see the latest committed write.

questions.q: PACELC extends CAP by noting that without a partition you trade off…
questions.why: Even when healthy, waiting for replicas to agree adds latency; that's the everyday trade-off.

questions.q: Is 'CA' (consistent and available with no partition tolerance) a realistic choice for a distributed system?
options: Not really: networks do partition, so you must handle it
Yes, it's the most common choice
questions.why: Partition tolerance isn't optional across machines; CA only describes a single-node system.

questions.q: During a partition, an AP system would most likely…
options: Keep serving reads and writes, reconciling conflicts later
Switch to a single node permanently
questions.why: AP systems stay responsive and resolve divergence afterwards (e.g. last write wins or merging).

questions.q: What is the most common index structure in relational databases?
questions.why: B-trees keep keys sorted, supporting equality and range queries with O(log n) lookups.

questions.q: What is the cost of adding an index?
options: Slower writes and extra storage, since the index must be updated
questions.why: Every insert, update or delete also updates each index, so index what your queries need, not everything.

questions.q: A composite index on (user_id, created_at) helps most with…
questions.why: Composite indexes work left to right: filter on the first column, then sort or range on the next.

questions.q: When does a hash index beat a B-tree?
options: Exact-match lookups only, with no range queries
questions.why: Hash indexes are fast for equality but can't answer 'between' or ORDER BY.

questions.q: Which index type finds text by the words it contains?
options: An inverted index (full-text search, e.g. Elasticsearch)
A B-tree on the whole text
questions.why: Inverted indexes map each word to the documents containing it; LIKE '%word%' can't use a normal B-tree.

questions.q: Which index helps 'find restaurants within 2 km'?
options: A geospatial index (geohash, quadtree or R-tree)
questions.why: Spatial indexes group nearby points so proximity queries don't scan everything.

questions.q: What is a covering index?
options: An index that contains every column a query needs, so the table isn't read
questions.why: The query is answered from the index alone, saving extra lookups.

questions.q: Which query can't use an index on email efficiently?
options: WHERE lower(email) = ? (without a matching expression index)
questions.why: Wrapping the column in a function hides it from the index unless you index that expression.

questions.q: Why is indexing a boolean column alone usually unhelpful?
options: Low cardinality: each value matches a huge share of rows
questions.why: If half the rows match, a full scan is often as fast. Partial or composite indexes can help.

questions.q: In an interview, when should you mention indexes?
options: When a key query would otherwise scan a large table, naming the columns to index
questions.why: Saying 'index on (user_id, created_at) for the feed query' shows you connect the data model to access patterns.

questions.q: Roughly how fast is reading from memory compared with a network round trip within a data centre?
options: Memory is about 1,000× faster (nanoseconds vs ~0.5 ms)
questions.why: Memory access is ~100 ns; a round trip inside a data centre is ~0.5 ms. That's why caching in memory helps so much.

questions.q: Roughly how many seconds are in a day, useful for requests-per-second estimates?
questions.why: Round to 10^5: 100 million requests a day is about 1,000 requests per second.

questions.q: A single modern PostgreSQL server can typically handle…
options: Thousands to tens of thousands of simple queries per second
questions.why: Well-indexed single servers go far; don't shard before the numbers require it.

questions.q: Redis on one node can usually serve on the order of…
questions.why: In-memory stores handle very high throughput per node, which is why one cache cluster absorbs heavy reads.

questions.q: If 1 billion users each store 1 KB of profile data, that's about…
questions.why: 10^9 × 10^3 bytes = 10^12 bytes = 1 TB, which fits on a single large machine or a small cluster.

questions.q: How long does a round trip between continents (e.g. US to Europe) take?
questions.why: Distance and the speed of light put a floor on latency, which is why CDNs and regional deployments exist.

questions.q: Kafka can typically handle, per broker, about…
options: Hundreds of thousands to a million messages per second
questions.why: Sequential disk writes and batching give very high throughput; partitions scale it further.

questions.q: Why do back-of-the-envelope estimates matter in an interview?
options: They show whether you need sharding, caching or more machines, and justify design choices
questions.why: Quick numbers (QPS, storage, bandwidth) turn vague 'it needs to scale' into concrete decisions.

questions.q: A 5 MB image served 10,000 times a second needs about how much bandwidth?
options: About 50 GB/s, a job for a CDN
questions.why: 5 MB × 10^4 = 5 × 10^10 bytes/s = 50 GB/s, far beyond one server, so serve it from a CDN.

questions.q: Reading 1 MB sequentially from an SSD takes roughly…
questions.why: SSDs are fast for sequential reads; random reads and network hops dominate latency more often.

questions.q: Clients need new chat messages within a second. Which approach avoids wasteful empty requests?
options: A persistent connection such as WebSockets or SSE
questions.why: Persistent connections let the server push as soon as something happens, without clients repeatedly asking.

questions.q: With users connected to many different servers, how does a message reach the right connection?
options: A pub/sub layer (e.g. Redis pub/sub or Kafka) routes events to the server holding that user's connection
questions.why: Servers subscribe to topics for their connected users; publishers don't need to know which server a user is on.

questions.q: Why are WebSocket servers harder to scale than stateless HTTP servers?
options: Each server holds long-lived connections, so load balancing and deploys must handle sticky, stateful clients
questions.why: Connections are pinned to servers; you need connection registries, graceful draining and reconnection logic.

questions.q: When is simple polling actually a fine choice?
options: Updates are infrequent and a few seconds' delay is acceptable
questions.why: Polling is simple, cacheable and stateless; don't over-engineer when delay is acceptable.

questions.q: What should a client do when its real-time connection drops?
options: Reconnect with backoff and fetch what it missed since its last event ID
Reload all data from scratch every second
questions.why: Push channels are best-effort; resuming from a cursor or event ID avoids gaps.

questions.q: For a live comment stream on a video with a million viewers, what reduces fan-out cost?
options: Batching and sampling comments, and sharding viewers across servers subscribed to that video's topic
Sending each comment to each viewer individually from one server
Storing comments in the browser only
questions.why: Topic-based fan-out across many servers, plus batching, keeps per-message work manageable.

questions.q: Server-Sent Events are a good fit when…
options: Only the server pushes updates, such as live scores or notifications
You need binary game state both ways
questions.why: SSE is simple, works over plain HTTP and reconnects automatically, but it's one-way.

questions.q: Where should the source of truth for messages live in a real-time system?
options: In durable storage; the push channel only delivers notifications
questions.why: Connections are ephemeral. Persist first, then push, so reconnecting clients can catch up.

questions.q: What is 'fan-out on write' in feeds or notifications?
options: When something is posted, it's pushed to each follower's inbox immediately
Followers compute the feed when they open the app
questions.why: It makes reads fast but is expensive for accounts with millions of followers, which are often handled with fan-out on read instead.

questions.q: Peer-to-peer (e.g. WebRTC) is most useful for…
options: Audio/video calls where low latency matters and media can flow directly between users
questions.why: Media goes directly between peers when possible, with servers used for signalling and relaying when needed.

questions.q: Two users try to book the last seat at the same moment. What prevents double booking in one database?
options: A transaction with a row lock (SELECT … FOR UPDATE) or a conditional update
A cache with a long TTL
questions.why: The database serialises access to that row, so only one booking can succeed.

questions.q: What is optimistic concurrency control?
options: Read a version number, then update only if it hasn't changed; retry on conflict
questions.why: It avoids holding locks and works well when conflicts are rare: UPDATE … WHERE id = ? AND version = ?.

questions.q: When is pessimistic locking the better choice?
options: When conflicts are frequent, so retries would waste work
questions.why: If many writers compete for the same row, locking up front avoids repeated failed attempts.

questions.q: How do sites like Ticketmaster hold a seat while a user pays?
options: A short-lived reservation with an expiry (e.g. a TTL in Redis or a status with a timestamp)
Charging first and choosing seats later
Locking the database row for 10 minutes
questions.why: A timed hold keeps the seat unavailable to others without long database locks; it's released if payment doesn't finish.

questions.q: What does a distributed lock (e.g. via Redis or ZooKeeper) coordinate?
options: Exclusive access to a resource across many servers
questions.why: When the resource spans services or databases, a lock service ensures only one worker proceeds; locks need expiries to survive crashes.

questions.q: Why must distributed locks have a timeout?
options: So a crashed holder doesn't block everyone forever
Because Redis requires it for strings
questions.why: A lease that expires lets others proceed after a failure; fencing tokens stop a slow former holder from writing afterwards.

questions.q: For an auction with thousands of bids per second on one item, what helps?
options: Serialising bids per item, e.g. a queue or single-writer partition per auction, with conditional updates
Letting every server update the price freely
Caching the price and never checking
Accepting all bids and picking later at random
questions.why: Routing all bids for one item to one ordered stream removes races without global locks.

questions.q: What is a two-phase commit used for?
options: Making a transaction commit atomically across multiple databases
questions.why: All participants prepare, then commit together. It's correct but slow and can block, so sagas are often preferred.

questions.q: A saga handles a multi-service transaction by…
options: Running local steps in order and compensating (undoing) earlier steps if a later one fails
questions.why: Sagas trade strict atomicity for availability, using compensating actions such as refunds.

questions.q: In an interview, what's a good first answer to 'how do you prevent overselling'?
options: Keep the critical check-and-decrement inside one database transaction or atomic update
questions.why: Start with the simplest correct mechanism (atomic updates), then discuss scaling it if the numbers demand.

questions.q: An order involves payment, inventory and shipping services. What keeps the process reliable if a server crashes midway?
options: A durable workflow (orchestrator or workflow engine like Temporal) that records progress and resumes
One giant database transaction across services
questions.why: Durable execution persists each step, so a crash resumes where it left off instead of losing or repeating work.

questions.q: What is the difference between orchestration and choreography?
options: Orchestration has a central coordinator; choreography has services react to each other's events
questions.why: Orchestration is easier to follow and change; choreography reduces coupling but spreads the logic around.

questions.q: Why must steps in a multi-step workflow be idempotent?
options: Steps may be retried after failures, and must not charge or ship twice
questions.why: At-least-once execution is normal; idempotency makes retries safe.

questions.q: If shipping fails after payment succeeded, a saga would…
options: Run a compensating action such as a refund
questions.why: Each step has an undo so the overall process ends in a consistent state.

questions.q: How do you handle a step that waits for a human, like manager approval for days?
options: A workflow engine that can sleep durably and resume on a signal or timer
A thread that blocks for days
questions.why: Durable timers and signals let workflows wait for long periods without holding resources.

questions.q: What does an event-sourced approach store?
options: Every event that happened, from which current state is rebuilt
questions.why: The event log gives a full audit trail and lets you replay or build new views, at the cost of complexity.

questions.q: What is the 'transactional outbox' pattern?
options: Writing the event to an outbox table in the same DB transaction as the data change, then publishing it
A cache for outgoing HTTP calls
questions.why: It avoids the dual-write problem where the database update succeeds but the message publish fails (or vice versa).

questions.q: Where do failed messages usually go after repeated retries?
options: A dead letter queue for inspection and reprocessing
questions.why: DLQs keep poison messages from blocking the queue while preserving them for debugging.

questions.q: Why not use one distributed transaction across all services?
options: It couples services tightly, blocks on failures and scales poorly
questions.why: Sagas and workflows give reliability without global locks.

questions.q: In an interview, when should you bring up a workflow engine?
options: When a process has several steps across services, long waits, or needs guaranteed completion
questions.why: It signals you know how to make long-running business processes reliable.

questions.q: A read-heavy app (100 reads per write) is overloading its database. What's usually the first step?
options: Add indexes and caching for hot queries
questions.why: Cheap wins first: make each query efficient, then serve repeated reads from a cache.

questions.q: What do read replicas provide?
options: Copies of the database that serve reads, spreading read load
questions.why: Writes still go to the leader; replicas scale reads but may lag slightly behind.

questions.q: What's the main drawback of reading from replicas?
options: Replication lag: a replica may return slightly stale data
They are slower than the leader always
questions.why: Route reads that must be fresh (like right after a user's own write) to the leader.

questions.q: Which content belongs on a CDN?
options: Images, videos and static assets requested by many users
questions.why: CDNs cache shared content near users, cutting latency and origin load.

questions.q: What is a materialised view or precomputed read model?
options: Data computed ahead of time into the shape a screen needs
An index on a primary key
questions.why: Precomputing expensive results (like a feed or leaderboard) makes reads cheap; updates happen on writes or in the background.

questions.q: A celebrity's post is read millions of times a minute. What helps beyond a shared cache?
options: Caching it in many places (local caches, CDN) or replicating the hot key
Putting it on one special shard
Rate limiting all readers to zero
questions.why: Hot keys overload a single cache node; spreading copies spreads the load.

questions.q: Why is denormalisation common when scaling reads?
options: It avoids joins on the hot path by storing data in the shape it's read
questions.why: Reads become single lookups; the cost moves to writes, which must update duplicates.

questions.q: What is request coalescing?
options: Combining many identical in-flight requests so only one hits the backend
questions.why: It prevents a burst of identical misses from overloading the database, e.g. when a cache entry expires.

questions.q: Search queries over millions of documents are best served by…
options: A search index such as Elasticsearch, kept in sync from the main database
questions.why: Inverted indexes answer text queries quickly; syncing can use change data capture.

questions.q: In an interview, how do you justify a cache?
options: Point to the read/write ratio and latency targets from your estimates
questions.why: Tie the decision to numbers: '10:1 reads, 50 ms p99 target' makes the cache a reasoned choice.

questions.q: A single database can't keep up with millions of writes per second. What's the core technique?
options: Partition (shard) the data so writes spread across many machines
questions.why: Replicas and caches help reads; only partitioning spreads writes.

questions.q: How does a message queue help with write spikes?
options: It buffers bursts so consumers write at a steady rate
questions.why: Queues absorb spikes and decouple producers from slower storage, at the cost of some delay.

questions.q: Why batch writes?
options: Fewer, larger writes cut per-request overhead and increase throughput
To make each write faster to appear
questions.why: Databases and disks handle a few big writes far better than many tiny ones.

questions.q: Counting likes on a viral post with 100,000 likes per second: what avoids a hot row?
options: Shard the counter into several sub-counters and sum them on read (or aggregate in memory and flush)
questions.why: Spreading increments across counters removes contention on a single row.

questions.q: Which databases are designed for very high write throughput?
options: LSM-tree stores like Cassandra, which append writes sequentially
questions.why: Log-structured storage turns random writes into sequential ones, trading some read cost.

questions.q: What is write-behind (write-back) caching?
options: Writes go to the cache first and are flushed to the database later
questions.why: It gives fast writes but risks losing data if the cache fails before flushing.

questions.q: Why does the shard key matter even more for writes?
options: A key that sends most writes to one shard (e.g. today's date) creates a hotspot
questions.why: Evenly distributed keys spread write load; time-based keys concentrate it.

questions.q: What does back-pressure do?
options: Signals producers to slow down when consumers fall behind
questions.why: Without it, queues grow without limit or systems fall over under overload.

questions.q: For analytics events (clicks, views) at huge volume, a common design is…
options: Stream them into Kafka and aggregate with a stream processor into summarised tables
Insert each event into a relational table synchronously
questions.why: Streaming plus aggregation reduces billions of raw events to manageable, query-ready results.

questions.q: In an interview, what should you estimate before designing for write scale?
options: Peak writes per second and data size per write
questions.why: Numbers decide whether one database is enough or partitioning and queues are needed.

questions.q: How should clients upload large files like videos?
options: Directly to object storage using a pre-signed URL, bypassing your app servers
Through your API servers in one request
questions.why: Pre-signed URLs let clients upload straight to S3-like storage, so app servers don't carry gigabytes of traffic.

questions.q: What is a pre-signed URL?
options: A temporary URL granting limited permission to upload or download one object
questions.why: Your server signs it with an expiry; the client uses it without needing storage credentials.

questions.q: Why use multipart (chunked) uploads for large files?
options: Parts upload in parallel and failed parts can be retried without starting over
questions.why: Resumable, parallel uploads are faster and more reliable on flaky networks.

questions.q: How do you serve large files to many users worldwide?
options: Through a CDN in front of object storage
questions.why: CDNs cache content near users and absorb bandwidth.

questions.q: Where does the file's metadata (owner, name, size, status) go?
options: In a database, with a pointer to the object's storage key
questions.why: Databases handle queries and permissions; object storage holds the bytes.

questions.q: How does your system know an upload to object storage finished?
options: Storage event notifications (or the client confirming), which update the metadata status
questions.why: Event notifications trigger processing (like thumbnails or transcoding) once the object exists.

questions.q: What problem does content-addressed storage (naming chunks by their hash) help with?
options: Deduplication: identical chunks are stored once
questions.why: Services like Dropbox avoid storing duplicate data and only upload changed chunks.

questions.q: Why not stream large downloads through your application servers?
options: They'd spend bandwidth and connections on bytes instead of logic, limiting scale
questions.why: Let the storage/CDN serve bytes directly using signed download URLs.

questions.q: How do you keep private files private while using signed URLs?
options: Short expiries and checking permissions before issuing each URL
Putting the password in the URL
questions.why: The permission check happens when the URL is generated; the expiry limits how long it can be used.

questions.q: Video platforms usually process uploads by…
options: Transcoding into several resolutions asynchronously after upload
questions.why: Background workers produce adaptive-bitrate versions so playback suits each device and connection.

questions.q: A report takes 2 minutes to generate. How should the API respond?
options: Accept the job (e.g. 202 with a job ID), process it in the background, and let the client check status
Keep the HTTP request open for 2 minutes
questions.why: Asynchronous jobs keep APIs responsive and resilient to timeouts.

questions.q: What sits between the API and background workers?
options: A queue (e.g. SQS, Kafka, Redis-based) holding jobs
questions.why: Queues decouple accepting work from doing it and let you scale workers independently.

questions.q: How does the client find out the job is done?
options: Polling a status endpoint, or a push notification/webhook
It keeps a socket to the worker
questions.why: Store job status in a database; clients poll or receive a push when it changes.

questions.q: Why must job handlers be idempotent?
options: Queues deliver at least once, so a job may run twice
questions.why: Retries after crashes or timeouts are normal; repeating a job must be safe.

questions.q: What is a visibility timeout in a queue?
options: How long a job is hidden from other workers after one picks it up; it reappears if not finished
How long a message is stored
questions.why: If the worker dies, the job becomes visible again and another worker retries it.

questions.q: How do you scale background processing for bursts?
options: Auto-scale workers based on queue depth
questions.why: Queue length is a direct signal of backlog; more workers drain it faster.

questions.q: What should happen to a job that keeps failing?
options: After a few retries with backoff, move it to a dead letter queue
questions.why: This keeps the queue flowing and preserves failures for debugging.

questions.q: For jobs that must run at a specific time (e.g. reminders), you'd use…
options: A scheduler that stores due times and enqueues jobs when they're due
questions.why: Durable scheduling survives restarts and scales across workers.

questions.q: How do you report progress on a long job, like '45% done'?
options: The worker updates a status record periodically, which the client reads
questions.why: Progress is just state the worker writes and the API exposes.

questions.q: In an interview, what's the tell that a task needs this pattern?
options: It takes longer than a normal request should (seconds to hours) or can fail and be retried
questions.why: Anything slow or unreliable goes async: transcoding, exports, crawling, ML inference.

questions.q: Where does Redis keep its data primarily?
options: In memory, with optional persistence to disk
questions.why: Memory gives sub-millisecond access; snapshots (RDB) or an append-only file (AOF) add durability.

questions.q: Which Redis structure suits a leaderboard?
questions.why: Sorted sets keep members ordered by score with O(log n) updates and fast top-k queries.

questions.q: How can Redis implement a simple rate limiter?
options: INCR a key per user per time window with an expiry
questions.why: Atomic INCR plus EXPIRE counts requests per window; sorted sets can do sliding windows.

questions.q: What does Redis pub/sub NOT guarantee?
options: Delivery to subscribers that are offline: messages aren't stored
questions.why: Pub/sub is fire-and-forget; use Redis Streams or Kafka when you need persistence and replay.

questions.q: Why is Redis single-threaded command execution useful?
options: Each command is atomic, so operations like INCR don't race
questions.why: Commands run one at a time, giving atomicity without locks; Lua scripts extend this to multi-step logic.

questions.q: How does Redis Cluster spread data?
options: Keys map to 16,384 hash slots divided among nodes
questions.why: Hash slots let the cluster rebalance by moving slots between nodes.

questions.q: Which Redis feature supports proximity search (drivers near a rider)?
questions.why: Redis geo indexes points with geohashes stored in a sorted set.

questions.q: What's a risk of using Redis as your only database?
options: Data can be lost between persistence points, and memory limits dataset size
questions.why: It's excellent as a cache or for ephemeral state; durable systems of record usually live elsewhere.

questions.q: How can Redis act as a distributed lock?
options: SET key value NX PX <ttl>: only one client succeeds, and the lock expires
A sorted set of all servers
questions.why: NX makes the set conditional; the TTL releases the lock if the holder dies.

questions.q: HyperLogLog in Redis is used for…
options: Approximate counting of unique items with tiny memory
questions.why: It estimates distinct counts (e.g. unique visitors) with about 1% error using ~12 KB.

questions.q: What data structure powers Elasticsearch's full-text search?
options: An inverted index from terms to documents
questions.why: Inverted indexes find documents containing given words quickly.

questions.q: Should Elasticsearch usually be your primary source of truth?
options: No: keep data in a primary database and sync it into Elasticsearch
questions.why: It's optimised for search, not transactions; it's usually a secondary, rebuildable index.

questions.q: How is data commonly kept in sync from the main database to Elasticsearch?
options: Change data capture or a queue of updates
questions.why: CDC streams database changes to the index with low delay.

questions.q: What does an analyzer do?
options: Breaks text into tokens and normalises them (lowercasing, stemming)
questions.why: Analysis decides how text is indexed and matched, e.g. 'Running' matching 'run'.

questions.q: How does Elasticsearch scale?
options: Indexes are split into shards spread across nodes, with replicas
By using a bigger single CPU only
questions.why: Shards spread data and queries; replicas add read capacity and resilience.

questions.q: Are new documents searchable instantly in Elasticsearch?
options: Near real-time: new documents appear after a refresh (about 1 second by default)
questions.why: Indexing becomes searchable at the next refresh; that's usually fine for search.

questions.q: Which feature ranks results by relevance?
questions.why: Relevance scoring weighs term frequency and rarity to order results.

questions.q: Elasticsearch fits which interview problem best?
options: Searching posts by keyword (e.g. FB Post Search)
questions.why: Keyword search with filters and ranking is its core use.

questions.q: Why is deep pagination (page 10,000) expensive in Elasticsearch?
options: Each shard must collect and sort many results before discarding them
questions.why: Use search_after or scroll-style cursors instead of large offsets.

questions.q: Besides text, Elasticsearch can also do…
questions.why: Geo distance filters and aggregations make it useful for location search and analytics dashboards.

questions.q: What is Kafka at its core?
options: A distributed, durable, append-only log of messages organised into topics
questions.why: Producers append to topics; consumers read at their own pace and can replay.

questions.q: How does Kafka preserve message order?
options: Order is guaranteed within a partition, not across a whole topic
questions.why: Use a key (e.g. user ID) so related messages land in the same partition and stay ordered.

questions.q: What decides which partition a message goes to?
options: The message key's hash (or round-robin if there's no key)
questions.why: Keys keep related events together; choose them to avoid hot partitions.

questions.q: What is a consumer group?
options: Consumers sharing a topic's partitions so each message is processed by one member
questions.why: Adding consumers (up to the partition count) scales processing in parallel.

questions.q: Can a consumer re-read old messages in Kafka?
options: Yes, by resetting its offset, as long as messages are within retention
No, messages are deleted when read
questions.why: Retention keeps messages for a set time or size; replay helps recovery and backfills.

questions.q: What limits the parallelism of one consumer group?
questions.why: Each partition is read by one consumer in a group, so more partitions allow more parallel consumers.

questions.q: Kafka is a good choice when you need…
options: High-throughput event streaming with durability and replay
questions.why: Event pipelines, logs, analytics and decoupling services are its sweet spot.

questions.q: Kafka's default delivery guarantee to consumers is best described as…
options: At least once: design consumers to handle duplicates
Exactly once always, with no effort
questions.why: Exactly-once is possible within Kafka's transactions, but idempotent consumers are the safe design.

questions.q: How does Kafka stay durable if a broker fails?
options: Partitions are replicated to other brokers
It keeps data in client memory
questions.why: With a replication factor of 3, a leader failure promotes an in-sync replica.

questions.q: Why can one very popular key cause trouble in Kafka?
options: All its messages go to one partition, overloading one consumer
questions.why: Split hot keys (e.g. add a suffix) or aggregate before sending to spread the load.

questions.q: What problem does Temporal solve?
options: Running multi-step workflows reliably, resuming after crashes (durable execution)
questions.why: It records workflow progress so code continues from the last completed step after failures.

questions.q: In Temporal, what's the difference between a workflow and an activity?
options: Workflows orchestrate deterministic logic; activities do the side effects (API calls, DB writes)
questions.why: Workflows must be deterministic so they can be replayed; external work goes in retryable activities.

questions.q: Why must workflow code be deterministic?
options: Temporal replays the history to rebuild state, and replay must reach the same decisions
questions.why: Random numbers, current time and direct I/O must go through Temporal APIs or activities.

questions.q: How does Temporal handle a failing payment API call?
options: Activities retry automatically with a configurable policy
questions.why: Built-in retries with backoff make transient failures invisible to business logic.

questions.q: A workflow needs to wait 3 days for an approval. In Temporal you would…
options: Use a durable timer or wait for a signal; no resources are held while waiting
questions.why: Durable timers survive restarts and cost nothing while waiting.

questions.q: Which interview problems benefit from a workflow engine?
options: Order processing, payments or ride booking with several dependent steps
questions.why: Anything with multi-step, long-running, must-complete processes.

questions.q: What does a Temporal 'signal' do?
options: Sends an external event into a running workflow
questions.why: Signals let the outside world (like a user approving) influence a waiting workflow.

questions.q: Compared with building a saga by hand over queues, Temporal…
options: Keeps the sequence, retries and compensation in ordinary code with state persisted for you
questions.why: You write the process as code; Temporal handles durability. Activities should still be idempotent.

questions.q: Where is workflow state stored?
options: In Temporal's persistence layer as an event history
questions.why: The history is the durable record used for replay and visibility.

questions.q: What's a downside of adding Temporal?
options: Another system to run and learn, plus determinism rules for workflow code
questions.why: It's powerful but adds operational weight; use it when reliability of long processes matters.

questions.q: What is an API gateway's main job?
options: A single entry point that routes requests to the right backend service
questions.why: Clients talk to one endpoint; the gateway forwards to microservices.

questions.q: Which cross-cutting concerns often live in the gateway?
options: Authentication, rate limiting, logging and TLS termination
questions.why: Centralising them avoids repeating the same code in every service.

questions.q: How is an API gateway different from a load balancer?
options: A gateway routes by API path and applies policies; a load balancer spreads traffic across instances
questions.why: They often work together: gateway decides which service, load balancer picks an instance.

questions.q: What's a risk of putting too much in the gateway?
options: It becomes a bottleneck and a place where business logic gets tangled
It removes the need for services
questions.why: Keep it thin: routing and policies, not domain rules.

questions.q: In an interview, should you always draw an API gateway?
options: It's fine to include in a microservice design, but don't spend time on it unless it matters
It must be the first deep dive
questions.why: It's a standard box; focus deep dives on what's unique to the problem.

questions.q: How does a gateway help with rate limiting?
options: It can reject excess requests per client before they reach services
questions.why: Stopping abuse at the edge protects everything behind it.

questions.q: What does 'backend for frontend' mean?
options: Separate gateway layers tailored to each client type (web, mobile)
A frontend that runs on the server
questions.why: Each client gets responses shaped for its needs without burdening core services.

questions.q: Why must the gateway itself be highly available?
options: Every request passes through it, so if it's down, everything is down
questions.why: Run multiple instances behind a load balancer across zones.

questions.q: TLS termination at the gateway means…
options: HTTPS is decrypted at the gateway, and internal traffic can use simpler or separate encryption
questions.why: It centralises certificate handling; many systems still encrypt internal traffic too.

questions.q: Can a gateway aggregate responses from several services?
options: Yes, it can combine calls into one response for the client
questions.why: Aggregation reduces client round trips, though heavy aggregation belongs in a dedicated service.

questions.q: Cassandra is best known for…
options: Very high write throughput and linear scaling across many nodes
questions.why: Its log-structured storage and leaderless design handle huge write volumes.

questions.q: What decides which node stores a row?
options: The partition key, hashed onto a token ring
questions.why: Consistent hashing of the partition key spreads data and requests.

questions.q: What does the clustering key control?
options: The sort order of rows within a partition
questions.why: E.g. partition by chat_id, cluster by message timestamp so a chat's messages are stored in order.

questions.q: How should you design Cassandra tables?
options: One table per query pattern, duplicating data as needed
questions.why: Cassandra has no joins; you model each query's shape directly.

questions.q: What does tunable consistency mean in Cassandra?
options: Each read/write chooses how many replicas must respond (ONE, QUORUM, ALL)
questions.why: QUORUM reads and writes together give strong consistency; ONE favours speed and availability.

questions.q: Why is a partition key like 'country' a bad idea for user events?
options: A few countries would create huge, hot partitions
questions.why: Partitions should be many and bounded in size to spread load evenly.

questions.q: Cassandra's architecture is…
options: Leaderless: any node can accept reads and writes
questions.why: No single leader means no single point of failure; replicas reconcile differences.

questions.q: Which interview problem suits Cassandra?
options: Storing chat messages or activity events at massive scale
A bank ledger requiring multi-row transactions
questions.why: High-volume, append-heavy data read by key and time range fits well.

questions.q: How are conflicting writes resolved by default?
options: Last write wins, based on timestamps
questions.why: Simple and fast, but clock skew can matter; model data to avoid conflicts where it's important.

questions.q: Deletes in Cassandra create…
options: Tombstones that are cleaned up later during compaction
questions.why: Heavy deletes can slow reads until compaction removes tombstones, a known pitfall.

questions.q: DynamoDB is…
options: A fully managed key-value and document database on AWS
questions.why: AWS runs the servers, scaling and replication; you design keys and access patterns.

questions.q: What does a DynamoDB primary key consist of?
options: A partition key, optionally with a sort key
Any column you like per query
questions.why: The partition key spreads items; the sort key orders items within a partition for range queries.

questions.q: How do you query by an attribute other than the primary key?
options: Add a global secondary index (GSI) on that attribute
questions.why: GSIs support alternative access patterns; scans read the whole table and are costly.

questions.q: Are DynamoDB reads strongly consistent by default?
options: No, eventually consistent by default; strong reads are an option on the base table
questions.why: You can request strongly consistent reads (not on GSIs), which cost more.

questions.q: What DynamoDB feature supports 'do this only if the item is unchanged'?
questions.why: Condition expressions enable optimistic concurrency, e.g. booking only if a seat is still available.

questions.q: DynamoDB Streams provide…
options: A change log of item updates for triggers and syncing
questions.why: Streams feed Lambda functions or pipelines, e.g. syncing to a search index.

questions.q: What causes throttling in DynamoDB?
options: Hot partitions or exceeding provisioned capacity
questions.why: Spread traffic with high-cardinality partition keys, or use on-demand capacity.

questions.q: Does DynamoDB support transactions?
options: Yes, ACID transactions across multiple items (with limits)
questions.why: TransactWriteItems groups writes atomically, useful for things like inventory and orders.

questions.q: What does DynamoDB TTL do?
options: Automatically deletes items after an expiry time
questions.why: Great for sessions, temporary holds or expiring data without cleanup jobs.

questions.q: DAX is…
options: An in-memory cache in front of DynamoDB
questions.why: It gives microsecond reads for read-heavy workloads.

questions.q: Why is PostgreSQL a strong default in interviews?
options: ACID transactions, rich SQL, indexes and it scales further than many expect
questions.why: Start with Postgres unless a requirement clearly needs something else.

questions.q: How does Postgres let readers and writers avoid blocking each other?
options: MVCC: each transaction sees a snapshot of row versions
questions.why: Multi-version concurrency control keeps old row versions for concurrent readers; VACUUM cleans them later.

questions.q: How do you scale reads on Postgres?
options: Read replicas via streaming replication, plus caching
questions.why: Replicas serve reads; writes still go to one primary.

questions.q: Which feature supports storing and querying semi-structured data?
questions.why: JSONB lets you mix flexible documents with relational data and still index them.

questions.q: Which extension adds geospatial queries to Postgres?
questions.why: PostGIS provides spatial types and indexes for proximity search.

questions.q: How do you lock a row to prevent a concurrent update?
options: SELECT … FOR UPDATE inside a transaction
questions.why: The row stays locked until the transaction ends, preventing races like double booking.

questions.q: Postgres's built-in full-text search is…
options: Good for moderate needs; dedicated engines like Elasticsearch scale further
questions.why: tsvector/tsquery with GIN indexes cover many cases before adding Elasticsearch.

questions.q: Which isolation level prevents all anomalies but may abort transactions?
questions.why: Serializable makes transactions behave as if run one at a time, retrying on conflicts.

questions.q: What happens when a Postgres primary fails?
options: A replica is promoted (via failover tooling), possibly losing the last un-replicated writes if async
questions.why: Synchronous replication avoids loss at the cost of write latency.

questions.q: What does a partial index index?
options: Only rows matching a condition, e.g. WHERE status = 'active'
questions.why: Smaller, faster indexes for the rows queries actually target.

questions.q: Apache Flink is mainly used for…
options: Stateful stream processing of events in real time
questions.why: It computes aggregates, joins and alerts over continuous streams such as Kafka topics.

questions.q: What is a tumbling window?
options: Fixed-size, non-overlapping time buckets (e.g. counts per minute)
A window that overlaps every second
questions.why: Each event belongs to exactly one window; sliding windows overlap.

questions.q: Why does Flink distinguish event time from processing time?
options: Events can arrive late or out of order; event time uses when they actually happened
questions.why: Correct analytics (like ad clicks per minute) should group by when the event occurred.

questions.q: What are watermarks in Flink?
options: Markers estimating how far event time has progressed, deciding when a window can close
questions.why: They balance waiting for late events against producing results promptly.

questions.q: How does Flink recover state after a failure?
options: From periodic checkpoints, replaying input from the checkpointed position
questions.why: Checkpoints plus replayable sources like Kafka give exactly-once state semantics.

questions.q: Which interview problem is a natural fit for Flink?
options: Ad click aggregation or top-k trending in near real time
questions.why: Continuous aggregation over high-volume streams is its core use.

questions.q: Where does Flink keep operator state for large jobs?
options: In a state backend such as RocksDB, checkpointed to durable storage
questions.why: Local state is fast; checkpoints make it recoverable.

questions.q: How does Flink scale?
options: Operators run in parallel across task slots, often keyed by a field
questions.why: Keyed streams partition work so each parallel instance handles a subset of keys.

questions.q: How are late events handled after a window closes?
options: Allowed lateness can update results, or they go to a side output
They're sent back to the source
questions.why: You choose a policy: update, drop or redirect late data.

questions.q: Batch vs streaming: why might you run both?
options: Streaming gives fast approximate results; batch recomputes exact results later (reconciliation)
questions.why: Many analytics systems pair a real-time path with a periodic batch correction.

questions.q: What is ZooKeeper used for?
options: Coordination: configuration, leader election, locks and service membership
questions.why: It's a small, strongly consistent store for coordination data between distributed nodes.

questions.q: How does ZooKeeper stay consistent?
options: A leader orders writes, replicated to a majority (quorum) of servers
questions.why: Quorum-based replication means it keeps working as long as a majority is up.

questions.q: What is an ephemeral node (znode)?
options: A node that disappears when the client's session ends
questions.why: Ephemeral nodes track live members: if a server dies, its node vanishes and others notice.

questions.q: How is leader election done with ZooKeeper?
options: Clients create sequential ephemeral nodes; the lowest number is the leader
questions.why: If the leader's node disappears, the next in sequence takes over.

questions.q: What does a watch do?
options: Notifies a client when a znode changes
questions.why: Watches let services react to config or membership changes without polling.

questions.q: Why keep a ZooKeeper ensemble at an odd number of nodes (3 or 5)?
options: A majority is needed; odd sizes tolerate failures most efficiently
questions.why: 5 nodes tolerate 2 failures; 6 nodes still only tolerate 2.

questions.q: Should you store large data in ZooKeeper?
options: No: it's for small coordination data, not bulk storage
questions.why: Data lives in memory and every write goes through the leader; keep it small.

questions.q: Which systems historically relied on ZooKeeper?
questions.why: Newer Kafka versions use their own KRaft consensus instead.

questions.q: What's a modern alternative for coordination?
questions.why: etcd provides similar consistent key-value coordination using Raft.

questions.q: In an interview, when does coordination like ZooKeeper come up?
options: Assigning work to crawler or scheduler nodes, leader election, or tracking which servers are alive
questions.why: Any time nodes must agree on who does what.

questions.q: Why can't a normal B-tree on latitude and longitude answer 'nearby' queries well?
options: It orders one dimension at a time, so a 2-D radius search scans too much
questions.why: Spatial indexes group points by area so nearby points are found together.

questions.q: What is a geohash?
options: An encoding of a location into a string where shared prefixes mean nearby areas
questions.why: Longer prefixes mean smaller cells; searching a cell and its neighbours finds nearby points.

questions.q: Why search neighbouring geohash cells too?
options: A nearby point can sit just across a cell boundary with a different prefix
questions.why: Checking the 8 neighbours avoids missing points near edges.

questions.q: What does a quadtree do?
options: Recursively splits space into four quadrants, splitting denser areas more
questions.why: It adapts to density: cities get small cells, oceans big ones.

questions.q: Which tool gives proximity search out of the box?
options: PostGIS, Redis GEO, or Elasticsearch geo queries
questions.why: In interviews, naming an existing geo index is usually enough before discussing internals.

questions.q: For drivers whose locations change every few seconds, which store fits well?
options: An in-memory geo index such as Redis GEO, updated frequently
A relational table with no index
questions.why: Fast-changing locations need cheap updates; in-memory indexes handle that.

questions.q: For restaurants that rarely move, what's a good approach?
options: A geo index in the database or search engine, updated only when a restaurant changes
questions.why: Static data can live in PostGIS or Elasticsearch with filters like cuisine and rating.

questions.q: How does geohash precision relate to cell size?
questions.why: Choose a precision matching your search radius.

questions.q: How do you rank results after finding nearby candidates?
options: Compute exact distances for the candidates and sort (plus other signals like rating)
questions.why: The index narrows candidates cheaply; exact distance refines the order.

questions.q: What's a scaling approach for global geo data?
options: Partition by region or geohash prefix across nodes
One global table on one server
Put it in the CDN only
questions.why: Queries are local, so partitioning by area keeps each query on few nodes (watch dense-city hotspots).

questions.q: What kind of data are time series databases built for?
options: Timestamped measurements such as metrics, sensor readings or prices
questions.why: They optimise for appending data points over time and querying by time ranges.

questions.q: Why are writes to a time series database usually append-only?
options: New points arrive in time order and old points rarely change
questions.why: Append-heavy workloads allow compression and fast sequential writes.

questions.q: What is downsampling?
options: Keeping lower-resolution summaries of old data (e.g. hourly averages)
questions.why: Recent data at full detail, older data summarised, saves huge amounts of storage.

questions.q: Why do time series databases compress so well?
options: Consecutive values and timestamps are similar, so deltas are tiny
questions.why: Techniques like delta-of-delta encoding shrink data dramatically.

questions.q: What are retention policies?
options: Rules that delete or downsample data older than a set age
questions.why: Metrics from two years ago rarely need per-second detail.

questions.q: Which interview problem would use a time series database?
questions.why: Monitoring dashboards and price history are classic time series workloads.

questions.q: What is 'high cardinality' a problem for in time series databases?
options: Too many unique label combinations (e.g. per-user tags) creating huge numbers of series
questions.why: Each unique tag combination is a separate series; unbounded labels explode memory and indexes.

questions.q: Examples of time series databases include…
questions.why: TimescaleDB builds on Postgres; Prometheus is common for metrics.

questions.q: How are time series usually partitioned?
options: By time chunks (and often by series), so old chunks can be dropped cheaply
questions.why: Dropping a whole time chunk is far cheaper than deleting rows one by one.

questions.q: Typical queries on time series data are…
options: Aggregations over time windows (avg CPU per minute over the last day)
questions.why: They're optimised for range scans and rollups.

questions.q: What does a Bloom filter tell you?
options: An item is definitely not in the set, or probably is
questions.why: No false negatives, some false positives, using very little memory.

questions.q: A web crawler uses a Bloom filter to…
options: Cheaply skip URLs it has probably already seen
questions.why: Checking billions of URLs in memory avoids a database lookup for most of them.

questions.q: Count-Min Sketch estimates…
options: How often items appear in a stream, using fixed memory (may overestimate)
questions.why: Useful for heavy hitters and trending items like top-k videos.

questions.q: HyperLogLog estimates…
options: The number of distinct items (cardinality) with small memory
questions.why: About 1–2% error using kilobytes, e.g. unique visitors per day.

questions.q: Why use probabilistic data structures?
options: Exact answers would need too much memory or time at huge scale; small errors are acceptable
questions.why: Trading a little accuracy for massive savings is often worth it.

questions.q: Can you delete items from a standard Bloom filter?
options: No: bits are shared, so clearing one could remove others (counting Bloom filters allow it)
questions.why: Counting Bloom filters use counters instead of bits to support deletion.

questions.q: What controls a Bloom filter's false positive rate?
options: Its size in bits and the number of hash functions relative to items stored
questions.why: More bits per item lowers the false positive rate.

questions.q: Finding the top 10 trending hashtags in a stream of billions uses…
options: A Count-Min Sketch plus a small heap of candidates
questions.why: The sketch estimates counts; the heap tracks the current leaders.

questions.q: A skip list is used in…
options: Redis sorted sets and some databases, for ordered data with fast search
questions.why: Skip lists give O(log n) search, insert and range queries with simple code.

questions.q: In an interview, when should you mention these structures?
options: When exact answers at scale would be too expensive, like unique counts, dedup or top-k
questions.why: They show you can trade precision for scale deliberately.

questions.q: What does a vector database store and search?
options: Embeddings (lists of numbers) and finds the most similar ones
questions.why: Similar meaning becomes nearby vectors, enabling semantic search and recommendations.

questions.q: What is an embedding?
options: A numeric vector representing content, produced by a model, where similar content is close
questions.why: Text, images or users are mapped into the same space so distance means similarity.

questions.q: Why use approximate nearest neighbour (ANN) search?
options: Exact search over millions of high-dimensional vectors is too slow
It uses more memory for no reason
questions.why: ANN indexes like HNSW trade a little accuracy for large speed-ups.

questions.q: HNSW is…
options: A graph-based index that navigates layers of neighbours to find close vectors
questions.why: It's one of the most popular ANN algorithms for its speed and recall.

questions.q: Which similarity measures are common for embeddings?
options: Cosine similarity, dot product or Euclidean distance
questions.why: The choice matches how the embedding model was trained.

questions.q: Where do vector databases appear in AI applications?
options: Retrieval-augmented generation: finding relevant documents to give an LLM as context
questions.why: RAG retrieves the closest chunks to a query and includes them in the prompt.

questions.q: How do you combine vector search with filters (e.g. only English docs)?
options: Metadata filtering alongside the vector query (pre- or post-filtering)
questions.why: Most vector stores support filters; how they're applied affects recall and speed.

questions.q: Can PostgreSQL do vector search?
questions.why: pgvector is a pragmatic choice when data already lives in Postgres.

questions.q: What is 'recall' in ANN search?
options: The share of true nearest neighbours the index actually returns
questions.why: Tuning index parameters trades recall against speed and memory.

questions.q: Hybrid search combines…
options: Keyword (e.g. BM25) and vector similarity results
questions.why: Keywords catch exact terms; vectors catch meaning. Together they often rank best.

questions.q: What is change data capture (CDC)?
options: Streaming every insert, update and delete from a database to other systems
questions.why: Other systems (search, caches, analytics) stay in sync with the source of truth.

questions.q: Where does log-based CDC read changes from?
options: The database's write-ahead log / replication log
questions.why: Reading the log captures every committed change without adding load from polling queries.

questions.q: Which tool is a common CDC connector?
questions.why: Debezium reads Postgres/MySQL logs and emits change events.

questions.q: Why is CDC better than 'write to the DB, then also write to the search index' in app code?
options: It avoids the dual-write problem where one write succeeds and the other fails
questions.why: The database log is the single source of truth; downstream systems derive from it.

questions.q: Which use case suits CDC?
options: Keeping Elasticsearch in sync with Postgres
questions.why: Search indexes, caches and data warehouses are classic CDC consumers.

questions.q: What must CDC consumers handle?
options: Duplicates and ordering per key, so updates apply correctly
questions.why: At-least-once delivery means consumers should be idempotent, and order matters per row.

questions.q: How does CDC help with cache invalidation?
options: Change events trigger cache updates or deletes when data changes
questions.why: Invalidation driven by actual changes is more reliable than app code remembering to do it.

questions.q: What is the lag in CDC?
options: The delay between a change committing and consumers applying it, usually seconds or less
questions.why: Downstream views are eventually consistent; monitor lag.

questions.q: How does the outbox pattern relate to CDC?
options: Events written to an outbox table are published by CDC, reliably tied to the transaction
questions.why: CDC on the outbox table gives reliable event publishing without dual writes.

questions.q: What happens to CDC when the schema changes?
options: Consumers must handle new or changed fields; schema registries help manage versions
questions.why: Plan for schema evolution so downstream systems don't break.
